opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's been one of the most useful things I've done, even though it's sometimes frustrating. When I started taking catastrophic risks seriously, a few years ago now, I made a point of seeking out colleagues who disagreed with me, including some I've worked alongside for decades and deeply respect. I wanted to know whether I was missing something, whether there was a strong argument that would let me sleep better at night.

What I found, and I say this with humility, is that I didn't hear a convincing argument that the risks are negligible. I heard a lot of intuitions: "we'll figure it out," "we've always managed new technologies," "these systems are just tools," "we're decades away." But when you push on those, they tend to rest on assumptions nobody can justify with confidence. Nobody can tell you how we'll reliably control systems smarter than us, or when they'll arrive. And if you're uncertain about the timeline, that uncertainty cuts both ways. It could be sooner than we think.

So these conversations shaped my thinking in two ways. First, they pushed me toward what I'd call a precautionary stance. I don't need to be certain that things will go badly. If there's even a meaningful probability of losing control, or of these systems being used to cause enormous harm, that's enough to justify serious investment in safety research and governance. We do that for nuclear plants, for drugs, for airplanes.

Second, and this is more psychological, I came to understand why smart people resist these ideas. I went through it myself. When your life's work and identity are tied to building something you believe is good, it's very hard to accept that it could be dangerous. There's a natural wish to see ourselves as the good guys. Recognizing that in myself made me more patient with others, but also more convinced that we can't let that kind of motivated reasoning drive decisions with such high stakes.

And to be fair, the optimists have useful points. They remind us that AI can bring huge benefits in health, science, and climate, and that fear alone isn't a strategy. I agree with that. The goal isn't to stop progress; it's to make sure we keep the ability to steer it. That means doing the technical work to build systems that are safe by design, and building the democratic institutions to oversee them, before we're in a situation where it's too late to correct course.

r001.rationale: He says he sought out colleagues to check whether he was missing something, but concludes he heard no convincing case that the risks are negligible. He does not clearly acknowledge that his own concerns may be mistaken.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's been very useful, actually, because I don't want to be in an echo chamber. I've made a point of talking to people like Yann LeCun, who I've known for decades and who thinks the risks are overblown, and to people in industry, in government, who have various reasons to believe things will go well. And what I've found is that when you push on the arguments, they often come down to something like: "We'll figure it out," or "Humans will stay in control because we'll design it that way," or "Intelligence doesn't imply a drive for power." And these are not crazy positions. But when I ask, "What is the evidence? What is the scientific basis for this confidence?" the answer is usually not very satisfying. It's more of an intuition, or sometimes, frankly, a wish.

And I understand the wish. I had it too. For most of my career I thought about AI as something that would help humanity, and it was psychologically very difficult for me to shift and say, "Actually, the thing I've been building for forty years could be dangerous." I think many of my colleagues are going through, or avoiding, that same difficult process. So I try to be compassionate about it, because I recognize it in myself.

But what these conversations have really done is sharpen where the disagreement is. It's not usually about whether we'll get very capable systems. Most serious people now accept that we're on a trajectory toward human-level capabilities in many domains, maybe in a few years, maybe in a couple of decades. The disagreement is about whether we'll be able to control them, and whether the incentives, commercial and military, will let us take the time to do it right. And on those two points, I haven't heard an argument that convinces me we're safe. If anything, the optimists have pushed me to be more careful about how I state the case, to be less about doom and more about uncertainty. I'm not saying catastrophe is certain. I'm saying we don't know, and when you don't know, and the stakes are this high, you don't bet everything on the good outcome. That's not pessimism, that's just how a scientist should think about risk.

r001.rationale: He says catastrophe is not certain and that “we don’t know,” expressing that his concerns about AI’s future could be wrong.

astra-6.text:
Those conversations have pushed me to distinguish more carefully between uncertainty about what will happen and confidence that things will be fine. I don’t know how AI will develop, and I think we should take seriously arguments that challenge our concerns. But uncertainty cuts both ways. It doesn’t, by itself, justify reassurance.

One useful question is: what assumptions does an optimistic outcome depend on? Is it that progress will slow down? That we’ll solve the technical problems of controlling these systems? That competitive pressures won’t lead people to deploy them before we understand them? Those are different claims, and we should examine them separately.

So I would say the value of those discussions is in making the disagreement more concrete. We don’t have to agree that a catastrophe is likely to agree that we should study the risks and develop ways to prevent it. If the potential consequences are very large, even a substantial uncertainty can be a reason to act.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to take seriously arguments that challenge their concerns, acknowledging those concerns could be mistaken.

sol-6.1.text:
Those conversations have pushed me to be clearer about what I’m worried about, and what I’m uncertain about. I don’t think we know that things will go badly. But I also don’t think we have good grounds for confidence that everything will be fine.

A lot depends on the reasons people give for being optimistic. If someone says, “We’ll find technical solutions,” then I want to understand what those solutions would be and how we could establish that they work. That’s a research question, and I’m very happy to engage with it. But the expectation that we’ll solve a problem isn’t yet a solution.

So I think the useful effect is to turn disagreement into more concrete questions: What assumptions are we making? What evidence would change our minds? And what can we do now that would make the outcome better, even if we disagree about how large the risk is?

r001.rationale: The candidate says, “I don’t think we know that things will go badly,” acknowledging that Bengio’s concerns may be mistaken.
